#8269. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8266. Pinnacle Sunrise

Let the record show that I was on time, it was the sun that was early. The confusion doesn’t end there.

Call me uneducated, but I could have swore that the time of sunrise wasn’t an especially flexible thing. After a long night mostly in my tent, I was up and alert enough a little after 6:00AM. Sunset was scheduled for 6:44AM, give or take. I enjoyed a nice breakfast, started packing up, started filtering my remaining water, and, at precisely 6:40AM, headed back over to The Pinnacle from my nearby camping spot. The walk couldn’t have been more than a minute, but sure enough, Mr. sun was already halfway above the horizon! I checked my phone, 6:41AM. Classic. I mean, its not big deal, the best pictures are of the sun cresting the horizon, which I was still able to get from a few different positions on the various rocks jutting out over the valley. Still, I wanted my special morning moment where the sun first peers over the horizon. Today’s sunrise would be a brief event since clouds were out in force. The sun would soon be un-setting as it disappeared into them. It would be back out in a few hours as the clouds were expected to clear completely by noon.

After the sunrise it was time to make my next decision. I could extend today’s hike and head a bit further south to the Windsor Furnace Shelter and take the blue blaze shortcut back north. It would mean I wouldn’t be returning to The Pinnacle in my next hiking stint, but that might be OK since the weather looked cloudy on Wednesday and rainy on Thursday, there might not be much to see. But I also wanted to wrap up the hiking stint and get back to town. I lost track of the decision while packing up my tent and instinctively took the shorter route back the direction I came from. I blame the chilly morning for this choice, I wasn’t about to sign myself up for extra hiking while I was still trying to get warm. By the time I realized which way I was heading I just accepted it, maybe the weather would turn and I’d see something at The Pinnacle anyway.

Progress was swift on the gravel road leading all the way down to Eckville from The Pinnacle. What a thoughtful place for the trail, especially with the surplus of rocks around. In fact, it was too inviting, I managed to steam along the road until I looked up and realized that I was staring at a blue blaze. I knew immediately I was on the trail down to a parking lot and would need to backtrack uphill to rejoin the AT. By the time I was crossing the road in Eckville I had only just finished my water, so I didn’t feel the need to swing by the shelter for more. I had also already stopped to remove my sleeping layers which were helpful to keep me warm during the first hour or so of hiking, but now I’d be heading uphill and soon the temperature would be hitting the mid sixties. Long Johns would not be necessary.

I spotted a buck along the trail just before the climb back up to the ridge that I would be following all the way. Up on the ridge I had a clear view of The Pinnacle. The clouds were in full retreat. It was a little wild to think I’d woke up there this morning. It wasn’t even 10:00AM, I was making serious time. I put my head down and continued my cruise back to the van.

A buck enjoys the warmth of the sun by the trail.

Looking at The Pinnacle. I started there at 7:00AM and made it all the way here in less than 3 hours!

Looking at The Pinnacle from the trail north. I love how the blue sky creates the illusion that there is another mountain ridge behind it.

Despite the occasional rock-induced slowdowns, I couldn’t be stopped today. That is, except at the Thunderhead Lodge where I again found myself taking a blue blaze trail completely by accident. I decided to stick with this one since it was short and I could easily rejoin the AT once I reached route 309. The blue blaze took me straight to the Thunderhead Lodge which was closed, but the “bartender” was apparently still working. I requested a water refill, but the bartender just told me a joke about customers not being about to hold their liquor. I figured this was the way the establishment tells hikers they are closed and set off to rejoin the AT.

I made it all the way back to my van at 2:30PM. I hiked 21.8 miles of Appalachian Trail in 7.5 hours. The miles going the wrong way down the first blue blaze are not included, neither is time spent stopping for bathroom breaks, wardrobe adjustments, pictures etc. It is safe to say that I hiked at 3 miles an hour overall, a very respectable pace especially since there was some uphill and definitely some tricky rock sections to navigate through. That bodes well for my upcoming 4 state challenge attempt which will be quite time crunched and require sustaining a robust pace.

With plenty of time left in the day I headed to Reading, PA to put some time into my blog before heading back to the trail. I had been coordinating the return of the Z seat with Pebbles and Greasetrap, they are camping near the road so it should be easy to locate them and return the package to its owner tomorrow morning.

View from the trail near the New Tripoli Campsite.

#8265. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”

#8262. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#8260. Katie “Raven” Gunvalson Sets New Overall Self-Supported FKT Reported on Pinhoti Trail

Record-breaking news from the southeast this week. Although the attempt has yet to be verified, it appears the Pinhoti Trail will soon have a new self-supported Fastest Known Time (FKT).

On November 15, 2026, the Pinhoti Outdoor Center posted about the latest FKT. According to the post, Katie “Raven” Gunvalson covered the 350-mile Pinhoti Trail through Alabama and Georgia in 6 days, 14 hours, and 39 minutes. If verified, this attempt will establish a new overall self-supported record for the point-to-point route, which includes approximately 50,000 feet of elevation gain.

Pinhoti Outdoor Center’s Facebook post highlighting the pending record-setting FKT.

The previous women’s record was set in 2022 by Liz Derstine, with a time of 7 days, 18 hours, and 22 minutes. The previous men’s record, which also stood as the overall record, was set in 2020 by Willie Thacker, with a time of 6 days, 16 hours, and 7 minutes. Gunvalson’s 2026 effort shaved nearly two hours off Thacker’s record, establishing a new overall time to beat.

Gunvalson is no stranger to record-breaking efforts. She has set FKTs across the US, including the current female self-supported records on the Oregon Coast Trail and the Ouachita Trail. The Pinhoti Trail attempt would be her first overall record, establishing a new benchmark for all competitors.

FastestKnownTime.com, the official FKT website and record-verification platform, lists the Pinhoti Trail as 335 miles long. However, FarOut and other trail guides list its length at approximately 350 miles. Gunvalson’s tracking GPX file has yet to be published, so her total mileage has not been confirmed. New records can take several weeks to be verified and published on the website, so additional information should become available in the coming weeks.

According to FastestKnownTime.com’s guidelines, there are three distinct “styles” that indicate varying levels of outside assistance: unsupported, self-supported, and supported.

Unsupported means athletes receive no external assistance and must carry everything they need from start to finish. They may only collect water from natural sources.

Self-supported allows a little more flexibility, permitting athletes to accept assistance they can “manage or find along the way.” Self-supported athletes cannot have resources arranged specifically for them, but they can accept assistance available to other trail users, such as trail magic, hostels, and resupplying in town.

Supported efforts allow unlimited outside assistance, “as long as you are entirely self-powered.” For example, an athlete could receive food and water from a support crew but must continue moving under their own power.

Gunvalson’s Pinhoti attempt falls into the self-supported category. So far, there has been little coverage of the achievement, and details about her approach remain unclear. Did she resupply along the way? Did she stay overnight at a hostel? These logistical questions and others will likely be answered once the record is submitted and verified.

In addition to a GPX file, many athletes upload photos and commentary documenting their FKT attempts. In her previous records, Gunvalson has included daily mileage breakdowns, which readers may also be able to look forward to once this attempt is approved and published.

Photo of Katie “Raven” Gunvalson along the Pinhoti Trail. Photo from Pinhoti Trail Alliance’s Instagram.

The Pinhoti Trail was designated a National Recreation Trail in 1977. It spans approximately 350 miles from its southern terminus at Flagg Mountain in Alabama to its northern terminus in Georgia, where it connects with the Benton MacKaye Trail. Flagg Mountain is considered the southernmost peak of the Appalachian Mountain range and stands more than 1,000 feet above sea level.

The Pinhoti Trail is beloved by thru-hikers, section hikers, and day hikers alike. One of the most iconic thru-hikers in recent years even helped establish a hostel along the trail. M.J. “Nimblewill Nomad” Eberhart became the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail in 2021 at age 83. His record was broken this year by 91-year-old Dale “Grey Beard” Sanders.

Nimblewill Nomad, along with friends Lloyd and Tammy Caperton, recently opened the donation-based, “no-frills” Southern Comfort Hiker Hostel in Weogufka, Alabama.

A handful of adventurous hikers also use the Pinhoti as a connector on a border-to-border route along the East Coast known as the East Coast Trail. This route links the Florida Trail, Pinhoti Trail, Benton MacKaye Trail, Appalachian Trail, and International Appalachian Trail.

Since 2021, hikers and trail enthusiasts have flocked to Alabama for Pinhoti Fest, a festival created to promote and celebrate the trail. The Pinhoti is continuing to gain attention and popularity, and Gunvalson’s potential FKT will bring even more awareness to this southern footpath.

#8257. Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote.  “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#8254. A Different Hike: Camino in Reverse

We took our sweet time starting out this morning. Like true “hiker trash,” we were determined to take full advantage of the complimentary lobby perks at our hotel: free coffees, teas, and an automated orange squeezer that freshly crushed OJ right in front of you.

By 10:00 AM, we finally walked out into the busy streets of Millandoiro to begin the day’s trek. Unlike yesterday’s intimate trail options, this morning started on one main route heavily packed with pilgrims.

The twist? The entire throng was walking northbound toward Santiago de Compostela—meaning we were walking directly into the oncoming crowd.

When you hike in the same direction as everyone else, you rarely make direct eye contact with fellow walkers. Heading south against the traffic created a completely different dynamic.

For the pilgrims walking toward Santiago, encountering someone going the opposite direction was a rare novelty, so almost every single person looked up, made eye contact, and wanted to interact.

At first, we greeted everyone with a friendly “Hola,” “Buen Camino,” or “Bom Camino” (since we were on the Portuguese route). But after saying it every two minutes for an hour straight, Knockerz and I were mentally exhausted.

You simply cannot engage with hundreds—or thousands—of people every single day on a trail. We quickly vowed to drop our gaze, lock our eyes on the ground, and hike on like zombies.

It was a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60s. Even with our heads down, we kept physically bumping into people.

Because northbound pilgrims never expected anyone to be walking south, they rarely saw us coming. We spent half the morning doing an awkward “side-step shuffle dance” at every pass until we decided on a strict rule: always stick to the far right edge of the path.

To a long-distance hiker accustomed to a single marked trail, walking backward through a network like this takes constant focus.

Our route wound through narrow paved roads connecting medieval hamlets tucked into the hillsides. It felt like an endless labyrinth of cobblestone alleyways.

Because every arrow blaze was painted for northbound travelers, we constantly had to stop at intersections, turn around, and hunt for marks hidden behind stone walls.

To make matters busier, this section serves as the final 100 km for pilgrims on the Portuguese route seeking their Compostela certificates:

After our peaceful, quiet walk to Finisterre, jumping right back into the final 100 km circus was a shock to the system. We passed over a thousand people in the first two hours alone.

At one point, we took a single-track dirt path leading through a lovely forest. Noticeable red arrow blazes had replaced the blue ones, so we decided to follow them.

The path grew narrower and narrower, and soon we began spotting piles of toilet paper left behind by crowds unfamiliar with Leave No Trace (LNT) principles. Realizing we had strayed off the main route, we turned around and backtracked to the original junction.

We resumed our meander through ancient hamlets before spilling out onto a busy highway near A Escravitude, passing its grand yet worn-down cathedral along the roadside.

As the warm sun heated up the afternoon, we pushed through an eclectic mix of industrial zones, busy highways, railroad tracks, and quiet medieval villages.

With three miles left, the oncoming pilgrim traffic finally thinned out. But right on cue, we got turned around again inside a tiny medieval village with narrow pathways.

Rather than backtracking, we decided to test Google Maps to navigate through the alleyways back to the official trail:

Taking these brief detours through the “back country” turned out to be a great way to avoid the crowds, escape the trail litter, and explore off-the-beaten-path villages.

Before long, we reached Padrón. Because this town marks the starting point for many 100 km section-hikers heading north, we expect the heavy trail traffic to drop off significantly starting tomorrow.

After dumping our packs in our room, we wandered the narrow alleyways of this small medieval town. Under heavy renovation, the main cathedral was covered in scaffolding. A river walk led to a large old Roman bridge framed by a large convent on a hill.

We picked up dinner ingredients across the street, cooked in our shared kitchen, and settled in for the night. Walking the Camino Portuguese in reverse is proving to be vastly different from the Camino Francés—and heading the “wrong way” makes every mile a unique adventure.

#8251. Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

Published Nov 15, 2026 2:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 issue of Outdoor Life.

It was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life. I dropped him on a granite ridge in New York’s Hudson River Valley, where, on a clear day, you could see the Empire State Building 40 miles away. The buck was only a forkhorn, but I was beside myself with excitement.

Finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail. In those days, that feat often took some doing.

Back then, we knew next to nothing about white­tails. I worked as post forester and wildlife biologist for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point for eight years in the late ’60s and early ’70s, and one of my jobs was to manage the hunting program on the academy’s 16,000 acres in southern New York. I recall seeing large scratch marks under trees where some animal had pawed away leaves, but I had no clue what had done it or why. And neither did any­one else I talked to.

Then came new research as modern wildlife man­agement started to steamroll along, and we learned that those pawed areas were spots that somehow were linked to whitetail bucks before and during the rut. Now we call those disturbed areas “scrapes,” as every whitetail hunter from age 8 to 80 knows. Along with the research came the inevitable desire to “improve” whitetails and grow bucks with bigger and bigger racks. Studies on nutrition and genetics unearthed the means to grow super bucks. Intensive management was suddenly the name of the game around the country. People devel­oped genetically altered monster bucks, put up fences to contain them and began to sell their semen for about as much as my pickup truck cost. Since then breeding has become big business. And in some circles, hunting has become a matter of horn inches rather than the experience itself.

Am I complaining? Not at all. In fact, some good pals of mine run commercial whitetail preserves where intense management produces big racks for their clients. That’s their business. And it’s here to stay. I simply see it as a sad commentary when we focus on the size of the rack rather than the smells, sights, and sounds of a damp oak forest and the raucous cries of jays and crows. Everything in the woods contributes to the total experience — and if a spike or forkhorn buck shows up, then you can be proud to flip off the safety, squeeze the trigger and smile all the way home.

Happily, this big-buck syn­drome hasn’t affected everyone yet. Plenty of hunters, young and old, are still thrilled to down a forkhorn buck, but new management concepts threaten the option of taking younger bucks. Biologically speaking, it’s indeed smart to let the younger bucks in some habitats live another year or two. My problem with the new techniques is that we continue to focus on the size of the antlers.

Proponents of associations that pro­mote minimum antler restrictions steadfastly insist they aren’t focusing on trophy deer. But it seems to me that when you require a deer to be of a cer­tain size before you can shoot it, it’s trophy hunting, pure and simple. Yes, these techniques work in some areas; it just bothers me that we are forced to adhere to those rules. Call me old­fashioned if you like, but I hanker for the good old days.

Read Next: Why Do I Hunt? The Answer to Hunting’s Toughest Question

I wrote about this subject recently and a reader wrote back and called me a hypocrite. He said that I write for OUTDOOR LIFE and that this magazine endorses trophy-buck hunt­ing. Well, hellooooo. Show me a hunting magazine that doesn’t promote big-buck hunting. There aren’t any. Show me a magazine with a forkhorn buck on the cover. There might have been one, once, but I never saw it.

It’s human nature to appreciate qual­ity. That’s why the Guinness Book of World Records and the Miss America pageant have such appeal. We admire the biggest, the best.

A hunter who gets a truly big buck, even when it’s total luck, becomes an instant hero. He endorses products, appears in ads, gives seminars and is a big name in hunting circles. The vast majority of these trophy owners just happened to be at the right place at the right time. Most did not “pattern” the buck, watching it for months before the season and discovering what trails it used. The lucky person was simply in the correct tree stand when the buck happened to walk by.

Whitetail hunting today is totally for­eign to what it was when I killed my first buck. In much of the country, farm­ing practices and more restrictive hunt­ing produces older bucks with larger antlers. High fences and nutritional supplements aren’t necessary in those places. Pals who live in the Midwest, for example, say that a few decades ago they never saw the likes of the bucks running around now. I’ve been hunting Iowa for years. The size of the bucks showing up these days is scary.

All of us would like to shoot a big buck, myself included. Personally, I have a problem with antlers. When I see them, as long as they’re legal, the rifle is likely to swing up to my shoulder. There are exceptions, such as on a recent hunt in Kansas where I was told all sorts of 150-class bucks were waltzing around. I never saw one. I passed on plenty of other dandy bucks, ended up never firing a shot and cussed myself all the way home. Then there was the time in Saskatchewan, when a buck scoring 162 walked under my stand. It was pure dumb luck. I shot him, and I’m proud of him, and he’s my biggest buck ever, but I’m even more proud of a little six­pointer that hangs next to him.

But that’s another story. As they say, a trophy is in the eye of the beholder. That’s the bottom line.

#8249. A Thru-Hiker Turned Her Trail Recordings Into an Interactive PCT Sound Map

When Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz hiked the PCT in 2025, she wanted to create something that would outlast the hike itself: a record of the trail’s sounds, a snapshot of its changing ecosystems, and a way for people who might never get to hike the PCT to experience the trail for themselves.

Together with her friend and former business partner Haiden McGill, Wozniewicz turned hours of audio recordings taken along the PCT into Offbeat, an interactive sound map of the trail. The project features 74 recordings spanning nearly 1,800 miles from the Mexican border to Sky Lakes Wilderness in Oregon, where an overuse injury ended Wozniewicz’s hike early.

Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz on the PCT. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz

McGill and Wozniewicz both have backgrounds in audio engineering. The pair met in college and founded a sound design company together at age 20 and ran it successfully for four years.

“When I got back from the PCT, all I had was an SD card full of audio files and an ambitious idea, but I knew there was exactly one person who could help me turn that idea into reality,” Wozniewicz told The Trek. That person was McGill.

“When Anna first mentioned she wanted to build an experience to showcase her recordings from the trail, I immediately saw the entire thing in my head,” McGill said of the Offbeat project. “The challenge was that I wanted the user to actually ‘hike’ the trail, not fly from place to place.” They set out to design a web experience that would feel both immersive and meditative, centering the sounds themselves.

Wozniewicz came off the trail with 137 separate audio recordings, and the pair have spent the last year turning those raw files into something more polished. Each of the 74 sounds that made it onto the Offbeat website is carefully edited into a seamless loop with no beginning or end, and a user scrolling through the sound map finds themselves meandering northward — indeed, much like a hiker would.

“Sound is subliminal, and we live in a very visual world. Throughout the build there was a constant temptation to add more visuals and UI elements to ‘enhance’ the story. This project was an exercise in restraint: keeping the listening experience calm and uncluttered. Instead of adding things, I used subtle camera movements, which I picked up from our filmmaking days, to draw listeners in and give the experience a meditative feel,” McGill said.

“I didn’t go into my hike with the intention to create Offbeat, but whenever I stumbled upon a cool sound, I got my recorder out and started recording,” Wozniewicz said. All she had with her was a cheap, lightweight Zoom H1essential recorder that she’d bought last-minute before her hike, but it was enough. “If you ask the UL bros, (it weighed) far too much, but in my opinion, it was surprisingly little.”

Her guiding principle, she said, was to capture sounds that would be hard to find in any other context — wind inside a hollow tree trunk, footsteps crunching up the icy ascent to Forester Pass, and an apocalyptic thunderstorm on Hat Creek Rim being some of her favorites. “It became kind of a game, to try and find the coolest, most unique sound I could each day.”

She aimed to capture natural sounds and, most of the time, exclude mechanical ones like traffic and airplanes. The hardest thing to capture? The silence. “Sometimes, the silence was overwhelming — no wind, no bugs, no rustling anywhere — this was the one sound (or lack thereof) that was impossible to record, that I feel isn’t represented in Offbeat, yet occurred pretty frequently on trail.”

Wozniewicz with her recording device. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz

Wozniewicz started to envision Offbeat about three months into the hike. “Hearing a specific sound can bring you back to a specific time, place, or memory. I’ve seen the PCT documented ad nauseam through images and video, but rarely have its sounds been captured, so it felt like a gap that I felt compelled to fill. My primary goal with Offbeat was to recreate the meditative experience of being in the wilderness.”

She hoped the project would evoke that feeling for others. “Getting to spend half a year just walking is an immense privilege, and many people will never get the chance to do something like that, so my hope is that Offbeat can bring the trail a little closer to a lot more people for whom a thru-hike isn’t possible.”

Navigating Sierra snowpack. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz

Offbeat is also intended to preserve an auditory record of the PCT’s diverse ecosystems, many of which are threatened by climate change. “Maps are a gift from the people who went before us, and I love that as a metaphor for continuing stewardship: you inherit the way, and you leave it better for the next person. In that sense, Offbeat is an archive we may soon look back on,” said McGill.

“Also — recognizing that I’m not even close to being the first (or last) person to hike the PCT corridor was important to me, which is why in the Audio Library view I’ve included the names of the Native peoples whose land each recording comes from,” Wozniewicz added.

Climbing Mt. Whitney. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz

Interestingly, Offbeat isn’t the only PCT sound library to come out this year. Field recordist Tom Kelly hiked the PCT in 2023 with over two pounds of recording equipment and just launched his own PCT sound map earlier this fall, featuring nearly 200 recordings up and down the trail. Like Wozniewicz and McGill, Kelly aimed to create a resource that would help people far from the PCT feel connected to the trail.

Wozniewicz and McGill could imagine doing a similar project on another long-distance trail someday. First, though, Wozniewicz wants to finish off the remaining miles of the PCT — and bring Offbeat’s audio pins as far north as the Canadian border. McGill said they hope to join for at least part of the remaining section.

“I’ve never felt more present in my life than on the PCT, and Offbeat is my way of packaging all those feelings up and sharing them with others,” Wozniewicz said.

Featured image courtesy of Anna Wozniewicz.

#8247. How to Soap-Tan a Rabbit Hide at Home

Published Nov 15, 2026 6:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

During the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do. Especially right after a fresh snow—there’s nothing like flinging arrows at cottontails.

Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.

I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend. So, I decided to tan the rabbit hides on my own.

I have tanned several deer hides, squirrels, fox, coyote, and mink. Rabbit, however, is a completely different story. If you’ve ever skinned a cottontail rabbit, you’ll know that their hides are the “tissue paper” of furbearing animals. Their skin is so thin and delicate that you can easily skin them without using a knife.

There are many ways to tan animal hides, and it can be overwhelming. Even once you decide on a specific method, there are various ways to approach it. After several nights of scouring the internet, including many taxidermy sites, I discovered a method called soap tanning that looked like it might work for rabbits. All the instructions I found were vague, but the process seemed simple enough. Not only does this method use simple household items, but it’s free of harsh chemicals. That means it’s safe to do indoors, and with small children and animals around.

The whole process, excluding the drying, only took me about an hour from start to finish. It was very simple, and the hide came out beautifully. So, don’t toss those bunny furs next time you bag a few—save and tan them! You can tan the hides fresh, or put them in a Ziploc bag and freeze them until you’re ready to start the process. Thaw 24 hours prior to tanning.

The first step is probably the most difficult step because, as I noted above, rabbit hide is very thin and tears easily. Most hides are fleshed with a fleshing tool, but that doesn’t work for rabbit hides as it would destroy the thin skin. Working slowly is the best way to avoid tears, but if you do end up tearing the hide, it can be fixed later.

Place the hide fur-side down, flesh-side up on your board. Using the tacks (or nails, like I did) pin the rabbit hide to the board. You’ll want the hide to be taut, but don’t try to stretch it too much. Your hide may be an odd shape, but that’s okay. That will be fixed later, and it’s better to leave it oddly shaped for now.

Once the hide is in place, use the flat side of a butter knife to gently scrape up the layer of flesh from the hide. The flesh will be slightly pink, and the hide underneath will be black and white. Hold the knife horizontal, keeping it as parallel to the hide as much as possible.

Once you’ve scraped enough away, you can grab the flesh with your hands and slowly peel it back from the hide, a little at a time to prevent tearing. Once you do this a few times, this goes fairly quickly. Be extra careful around holes in the hide that have been left behind from bullets or broadheads.

Once all the flesh has been peeled from the hide, remove the nails from the hide, and remove the hide from the board.

Place the hide in a clean bowl or bucket, and add a cup of olive oil. The measurement isn’t really important; just add enough to saturate the hide. Using your hands, work the oil into the skin side (not the hair) until you see the skin start to turn translucent. Don’t worry if you get oil on the hair side, though, since you’ll wash it in the next step.

In another clean bowl or bucket, add enough room temperature water to submerge the hide completely.

Add a healthy dose of dish soap (I used roughly half of a bottle). Again, measurements aren’t extremely important, you just want a strong ratio of soap to water.

Using a large wooden spoon or your hands, gently stir the hide in the soap and water. I started with a spoon and found it easier to use my hands. Be careful not to stir too vigorously, as this will make any holes in the hide even bigger.

Keep stirring the hide until the skin side starts turning white. Once all areas have gone from translucent to white, you’re going to test a small piece.

Do this by bringing a small pot of water to a boil. Trim a small piece of the rabbit hide that’s roughly 2- x ½-inch. (This is a great way to use a ragged edge that you want to trim off to fix the shape.)

Drop it into the pot of boiling water and leave it for approximately 30 seconds. Then use tongs to remove the hide and let it rest on a towel for a second. If the hide curls and is stiff, add more soap to your soap and water solution, and continue stirring. If the hide comes out of the boiling water and is still soft and pliable, your soap tan is complete.

Take your hide out of the soap and water solution, and run it under room-temperature water until all the soap is gone. Gently squeeze the hide to remove as much excess water as possible.

At this point, you’ll be able to trim the edges of your hide if you so choose. You’ll also want to sew any holes in the hide.

Cut a piece of thread about a foot long. Make a small knot in the one end of your thread, and thread the opposite end through your needle. You’ll want to use a simple whip stitch on the skin side to close the holes. Keep your stitches snug, but not so tight that the skin puckers. The edges of the hole should touch, but not overlap. This will result in smooth fur on the opposite side, with no lumps and bumps.

This is the longest part of the process. It took roughly 24 hours for the rabbit hide to dry completely. You’ll want to keep it in a dry area, away from pets and make sure no mice or rodents can get to it.

Hanging it on a hook or draping it over a rack so air can get to both the skin and fur side will ensure even drying. The hide will probably shrink a bit as it dries, but this is normal.

You can soften the hide during the drying process, or after. Trying to stretch a rabbit hide just rips it in half, so simply folding it and rolling it into a ball is the easiest way to soften the hide and make it more supple. If you skip this step, however, your hide will still be extremely easy to work with if you are going to use it for a sewing project.

The final step to tanning many hides is to smoke the hide over smoldering coals. Wet hides tend to dry stiff, even if they’ve been worked really well, and the smoke essentially “finishes” the hide in case it were ever to get water on it.

I chose to skip this step, as I plan on making a blanket once I have enough pelts, and it’s fairly unlikely that the blanket will ever get wet. On top of that, rabbit hides are so thin that even if they were to stiffen, they would still be very pliable.

If you do choose to smoke your rabbit hide, it only takes about 30 minutes. Keep in mind that smoking will change the color of the hide.

Read Next: Hunting Rabbits is the Perfect Cure for Winter Cabin Fever

Decide what you want to do with the hide. The possibilities are endless, whether you choose to display the hide on an end table, create fur trim on a garment, or save a dozen to create a pillow or blanket.

#8244. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

Published Nov 16, 2026 9:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

Wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

Whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

Another important point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”

Body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of new-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

Say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Big.”

Suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

After sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

The scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

One of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

This shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

Hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

Yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

Late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

But where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

Two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

In the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

Whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer quickly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

One day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then quickly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

In addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

However, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

First, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

Cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

Hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

Conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

Never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

Another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he quickly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck

Because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

When hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and plan your strategy accordingly.

This story was originally published in the November 1987 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8243. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

#8241. Day 36: Solitude Before the End

I woke up to my alarm at 4:30, tired but excited for the adventure of the morning.

In the same way I had the crazy idea of walking all night to Cruz del Ferro, my Argentinian brother had one of his own: meditating in the forest at sunrise. It took a bit of investigation, but we decided on going to the forest near Portomarín.

As I waited in the common room of the albergue, I was curled up with my headlamp on in the darkness. Another pilgrim joined me, offered me an instant coffee, and proceeded to give me fantastic advice about Santiago and the route after. This was his eleventh Camino, and he said,

“I always say it’s going to be the last one, but I keep coming back.”

My brother woke up, we stepped into the cloudy darkness, and walked toward the river in the valley. The long, long bank on either side was covered in knee-high plants that I could feel were leaving stickers in my pants.

I felt his hesitancy as he changed his mind on the route and we turned around to walk on the road.

What if we did it in the forest by Santiago after we finished?

I pulled out my map, double-checked that it could be a possibility, and brought it up.

Mother Nature told us to wait, giving the idea more time to simmer over the next few days.

It was a blessing in disguise because a few minutes after we made that decision, my Australian friend called me and invited us to breakfast.

All three of us sat together in her modern and elegant albergue while the employee took such good care of us.

Once we had our fill, we all hit the trail together.

As we walked and talked, the lush green grass and trees came in and out of view. The clouds were so dense at some points that we couldn’t see twenty feet in front of us.

While we walked, the craving for solitude crept up again. I just didn’t know how to say it.

We stopped at the first cafe open on a Sunday, two hours into the walk, and drank hot coffee outside while my brother and I attempted to lighten our packs with all the food we were carrying.

When I told him privately that I didn’t know how to ask the Australian friend for space, he encouraged me in Spanish not to “ask” but just “say”.

My brother and I started together, easily reading the other person without words. Between speaking in Spanish, English, or walking in silence, it was the perfect balance.

But he remembered I wanted to walk alone, gave me a hug, and stopped so I could go ahead. When I walked away, he taught me the old, traditional Camino phrase:

While I walked alone, I thought about the past few hours. My Argentinian brother really was my teacher, not only in Spanish, but also in how to be a more compassionate, more grounded human being. We all joked around that he looked like Jesus, but he might be one of the most “Christ-like” people I’ve ever met.

I felt so amazing during my solitude. I met and walked briefly with new people and ones I’d known before. Each time, after a bit of chatting, I let them walk ahead and came back to myself.

When I arrived in the town of Palas de Rei, the first albergue I went to was full, with the person right in front of me in line. I sat on a bench outside and decided to pivot.

The next cheapest option was Albergue Restaurante Castro. Only €5 more, I got real sheets, a memory foam pillow, and a curtain for my bunk. This felt luxurious compared to what I was used to. And with that, I fell right asleep.

When I awoke around 4, I grabbed the food I’d carried all day—half baguette, tuna, tomato, and mayo—and went to the church at the top of the town.

There, I ate my dinner overlooking the uneventful town. This was the first dinner I’d had alone in almost two weeks. The brothers weren’t with me, and it felt so strange. It felt like the universe saying,

“You wanted to be alone. Do you remember this?”

A few people nearby were speaking English, so I chimed in. The people from North Carolina looked shocked and amazed when I told them I had been walking since France. They were an example of the many people around me who were doing the last 100 km. Right before they left, one of them walked over to me and handed me a ceramic scallop shell she made.

“You’re the first person I’ve met who did the whole thing and I want you to have the first one.”

I strolled around town, trying to see if there was anything interesting to find on a Sunday evening. I ran into my Australian friend, then my Italian brother. My brother and I bought some gelato, sat in the plaza, and talked about the next week.

As he walked back to his albergue, I saw the sadness in his eyes behind a fake smile.

It was an early night, but I knew it’d charge my battery up for the intensity of the end.
